title: I'm a French dad with a full-time job. I built an idle RPG with AI in my free time. Last week it went from 35 to 430 concurrent players.
author: Sure_Yam7050
selftext:
English isn't my first language, so bear with me.

I have a full-time job, a wife and a kid. In February I started building a dark fantasy idle RPG in the evenings and on weekends. I wasn't trying to start a business. I just wanted to make the game I wanted to play.

I'll be upfront about AI because this sub is the right place for it. Claude Code writes almost all of the code. The art is AI-generated, then reworked and unified so it looks like one game instead of a pile of images. My job is everything around it: the design, the balancing, the testing, deciding what's fun and what isn't, and answering players at midnight when something breaks. AI made this possible with a family and a day job. It didn't make it easy.

**April to October: the quiet part, and the real work**

The game went live on its own website, [aethyridle.com](http://aethyridle.com), in April. For seven months it stayed small. My record was 35 players online at the same time. About 6,800 accounts were created during the beta, and I made about €1,200 in total. Six months of nights for €1,200.

But those months are where the game actually became a game.

The first version looked like what it was: a pile of AI images that didn't belong together. So I regenerated every monster and character portrait in the game, and I kept going until I found an art direction I was really happy with. Every new image now has to fit it, or it doesn't go in.

Then I redesigned every screen of the game. At one point I realized my screens looked too much like other idle games, not in the colors but in the layout itself. So I rebuilt how the screens are organized while keeping the art. I also threw away redesigns I had spent days on, because the old version was simply better. That hurt, but it was the right call.

All of that came out as version 2.0, with every screen redesigned, and my players loved it. That update is when I started to believe the game could go further than a small website. The players who stayed during those months taught me how to make this game, and they're still the first ones I listen to.

**Steam: harder than I expected**

I thought putting a web game on Steam would take a weekend. It took months.

The game had to become a real desktop app. My first build was rejected by Valve. The payment system I used on my website isn't allowed inside a Steam game, so I had to rebuild every purchase through Steam's own system. Login had to work with Steam accounts, and a player had to be able to keep the same save between Steam and the browser. Plus 100 Steam achievements, and a demo released before launch. The demo took me from 380 wishlists to 1,655 by launch week.

None of this is visible to players when it works. That's the point, but it's a lot of invisible work.

**November 2nd: launch**

I launched on Steam, free to play, with $0 in ads. I knew a Steam launch could bring a lot more people than my website ever did, so I prepared the servers for it: upgraded the database ahead of time and watched the load all day.

Then I watched the counter go past 100, 200, 300... and peak above 430 concurrent players. More than 12 times my previous record. As I write this on a Sunday evening, about 420 people are playing right now. The servers didn't flinch, and honestly that's the part I'm proudest of.

First week, Steam and website combined:

* Daily active players went from 383 on launch day (the game opened late afternoon) to 1,174 on Saturday
* About 3,100 new accounts
* On Steam alone, 8,270 people added the game to their library and 2,477 actually launched it. With free to play, a lot of people grab it "for later", and the gap is bigger than I expected.
* Median playtime on Steam: 44 minutes
* 36 Steam reviews so far, 80% positive
* 7 languages: English, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese, Russian, Chinese

**The money, since everyone asks**

The game is free. About 90% of the revenue comes from an optional monthly supporter subscription. The rest comes from gem packs.

At first I tried to make money with cosmetics only. I sold basically nothing. So now the cosmetics are included in the subscription, along with things that make the game more comfortable and faster: more offline progress, a second activity running at the same time, more inventory space.

That's where my few negative reviews come from. Almost all of them are from people who played less than an hour and called the game "pay to win". I understand the reaction. But the game is entirely single-player, and the leaderboard is optional. Nobody is competing against your wallet. And a free game with nothing to buy doesn't exist for long: I'm one person, and I'd like this game to keep growing. Still, those reviews hurt a bit, because a handful of them weighs a lot on a small game.

Before launch I had fewer than 20 subscribers. Today there are 188.

Before Steam, it took me more than six months to make €1,200. After Steam, I passed that in less than 5 days. The first week landed around €1,850 gross, before Valve's cut and taxes. It's not "quit your job" money yet, but it completely changed how I see this project.

**What broke: players are crazy (I love them)**

I thought I had tested everything. Then hundreds of players arrived and tried things I would never have thought of.

My favorite one from this week: a player managed to break a toggle in the settings. Now "reduced motion" turns ON when the switch says OFF, and the other way around. I still don't fully know how they did it.

Players are also way faster than I planned. I balanced the game so reaching level 100 would take about two weeks. On day two, 8 players were already past level 100. Today it's 492, and the top player is level 311. Every content estimate I had was wrong, so now I measure everything on the live game instead of guessing.

Some players also kept an old version of the game open for days after a patch, and kept playing with the old rules. About a hundred of them, at one point. So I'm adding a screen that asks outdated versions to update before continuing.

Since launch, I've shipped a big patch almost every day, fixing everything players reported in the Steam discussions and on Discord. Players also send ideas: this week one asked for a search bar in an endgame skill tree and a way to remove single points instead of resetting everything. Both are in the next update.

**Saves: the boring part that matters most**

Offline progress, cloud saves, two devices on one account, the same save shared between Steam and the browser. During the beta I had a LOT of save problems, so before launch I spent weeks making saves as safe as I could. It paid off: launch week had far fewer save bugs than I feared. Not zero though. I guess you can never secure it enough.

**Cheaters: I let them play**

It's a single-player game, so someone editing their save doesn't hurt anyone else. I don't ban anyone from the game. I built tools that flag impossible progress, and I simply remove those players from the leaderboard. They keep their game, the leaderboard stays clean, and everyone is happy. It's the least stressful decision I've made on this project.

**What's next**

The 44-minute median tells me the first hour needs work, so that's my focus right now. Android is coming next, and if this keeps going well, an iPhone version after that.

If you've launched a free-to-play game on Steam, what moved your numbers in week two? And if you have questions about building a game like this with AI on top of a full-time job, ask away. I'll answer everything.

I didn't plan to write a novel, but here we are. Thanks to everyone who took the time to read it.

Steam: [https://store.steampowered.com/app/4843460/Aethyr\_Idle/?utm\_source=reddit&utm\_medium=post&utm\_campaign=aig](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4843460/Aethyr_Idle/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=aigamedev)
